activities.name: 36 Questions — Set I as a Lunch Warm-Up
activities.one_liner: Run only the first, lightest set of 12 questions from Aron et al.'s closeness-generating procedure as a short, low-vulnerability warm-up.
how_it_works: Pick one of you to start; alternate who answers first each question.

Work through Questions 1-12 of Set I only (e.g., 'Given the choice of anyone in the world, whom would you want as a dinner guest?' through 'If you could wake up tomorrow with any one quality or ability, what would it be?').
Skip question 11 ('tell your partner your life story in as much detail as possible') if time is truly tight — it's the one open-ended 4-minute item in the set and the easiest to cut.
Stop after Set I. Do not continue into Set II or III during this window — those escalate into much more vulnerable territory a lunch-break hard-stop can't safely hold (see window_contraindications).
Text or voice-note the next unanswered question to pick up where you left off next time.
activities.timezone_friction: Set I's questions are light (favorite meal, a secret hunch about how you'll die, etc.), so a 20-minute chunk survives a hard stop; tagged w2 and w4 because both are bounded, low-stakes windows where an unfinished set doesn't cost much. Not tagged w3: several Set I questions invite real back-and-forth that's awkward to hold hands-free while crossing streets.
activities.source_date: 2026-08-02 (access date; original questions from Aron et al., 1997)

activities.name: The 36 Questions (Aron et al.) — Full Escalating Run
activities.one_liner: The complete, three-set, closeness-generating procedure from the original 1997 study, run start to finish in one sitting.
how_it_works: Sit or lie somewhere you can both hold a phone or laptop steady and won't be interrupted for 60-90 minutes.
Work through Set I (Q1-12), Set II (Q13-24), then Set III (Q25-36) in order — the escalation is the mechanism, so don't skip ahead or reorder.
Alternate who answers first on each question; both partners answer every question.
Q11 and Q22 are timed items in the original design (a 4-minute life story; alternately sharing five positive traits) — hold each other to something close to those durations rather than rushing.

Optionally close with several minutes of sustained eye contact over video (see the separate eye-gaze entry) — this specific closer is not confirmed to be part of Aron's own published 1997 procedure; it entered popular use via later media coverage (see gaps).
Afterward, talk about what surprised you rather than moving straight to something else — the original study measured post-task closeness, and the debrief is where that shows up.
activities.timezone_friction: The original protocol runs ~45 min of Q&A; realistically 75-90 min including debrief. Only w6 (worth-the-cost event window) and w7 (the one unbounded, both-fresh day) can hold that without a hard stop truncating Set III mid-vulnerability, which is worse than not starting.
activities.source_date: 1997 (Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 23(4), 363-377); question wording cross-checked 2026-08-02

activities.name: Four-Minute Silent Eye-Gaze Closer
activities.one_liner: A few uninterrupted minutes of pure eye contact over video, no talking — borrowed from mutual-gaze research and popularly (though not verifiably originally) paired with the 36 Questions.
how_it_works: Prop the phone/laptop so your face fills the frame at a natural distance.
Agree on a duration out loud first — 2-4 minutes is the researched range; don't just wing it.
Set a silent timer. No talking, no looking away on purpose, no phone-checking.
Hold each other's gaze on-screen until the timer ends.
Say how it felt afterward — some people find it intense or funny at first; that's normal and part of the original findings on mutual gaze.
activities.timezone_friction: Low physical effort (no talking) but requires holding visual attention, so it fits the sleepy-but-not-asleep end of w1 and the fading end of w5 as a closer right before sign-off. Skipped w2/w3/w4: several minutes of sustained eye contact reads as conspicuously intimate and isn't feasible mobile, at a desk, or in public.

activities.name: One Love Map Question, Asked in Passing
activities.one_liner: Ask a single question about your partner's inner world — a favorite memory, a current worry, a hope — as a stand-alone daily habit rather than a sit-down session.
how_it_works: Pick one question you don't already know the answer to (Gottman's Love Maps concept: e.g. 'What's stressing you out most today?' or 'What's a childhood memory you haven't thought about in a while?').
Ask it in whatever window you're in — no need to announce it as an 'exercise.'
Let the answer be as short or long as the moment allows; this is intentionally low-commitment.
If you're using a written question source, one partner can read the question aloud even if only they have it in front of them.
Optionally text a follow-up thought later if the conversation got cut short by a hard stop.
tools_needed: Phone call, FaceTime audio, or a voice note
optionally a Love Maps-style question list
activities.timezone_friction: This is the micro-version of Gottman's Love Maps concept, built specifically for the constraints: audio-only and hands-free for w3 (her commute), short enough for w2 and w4's hard bounds. Not tagged w1/w5/w6/w7 — in those longer windows a single question undersells the available time.

activities.name: Weekly State of the Union Meeting
activities.one_liner: Gottman's structured four-part weekly meeting: appreciations, what's working, concerns via the ATTUNE framework, then one request each for the coming week.
how_it_works: Set a standing weekly time — w7 (Saturday) is the natural fit since it's the only day both of you are fully off.
Part 1: each of you shares five things you appreciated about the other from the past week.
Part 2: discuss together what's working or improving in the relationship right now.

Part 3: each of you raises any concerns from the week using the ATTUNE approach (Awareness, Tolerance, Turning Toward, Understanding, Non-defensive listening, Empathy) rather than jumping to problem-solving.
Part 4: each of you names one specific thing the other can do in the coming week to help you feel more connected.
tools_needed: optionally a notes doc to track recurring concerns/requests week to week
activities.timezone_friction: Requires both partners alert and willing to sit with a real concerns section — only w7, the sole symmetric-energy window, reliably provides that. See window_contraindications for why w1/w4/w5 are wrong for the concerns portion specifically.

activities.name: The Stress-Reducing Conversation
activities.one_liner: One partner vents about stress from OUTSIDE the relationship for a set stretch while the other just listens, validates, and takes their side — no fixing, no relationship topics.
how_it_works: Agree who complains first; the other is purely the listener for that stretch.
The complaining partner talks about a stressor from work, friends, or logistics — anything except the relationship itself; that's the one hard rule.
The listener doesn't offer solutions unless asked, shows understanding before anything else, validates even parts they might privately disagree with, and expresses a 'we against the problem' stance.
Swap roles if there's time; if not, save the other person's turn for the next call.
End without a resolution requirement — the goal is feeling heard, not fixing anything.
tools_needed: FaceTime audio or video; headphones acceptable
activities.timezone_friction: Matches w5's built-in split exactly — she's post-work and energized (natural complainer), he's fading (the listener role only requires receptive attention, not high output). Also fits w4: the rule against discussing the relationship itself keeps it low-risk for a bounded desk/lunch setting, and a quiet-voice/headphones version keeps it discreet.

activities.name: Rituals of Connection Audit
activities.one_liner: A sit-down conversation to explicitly name which small, repeatable moments of connection you already have and which ones you want to add.
how_it_works: Each of you separately lists the small, predictable moments that currently make you feel connected (a specific text, a call time, a shared show, a goodnight ritual).
Compare lists together and mark which ones are actually happening reliably vs. which have quietly lapsed.
Use Gottman's framing to sort them: rituals are emotionally meaningful and relationship-focused; routines are just task completion. A lapsed ritual is worth reviving; a lapsed routine usually isn't.
Pick 1-3 candidate rituals to commit to explicitly, including which window(s) of your overlap clock each one lives in.
Revisit this list every few months, since what counts as a ritual will shift as your schedules do.
activities.timezone_friction: This is a planning conversation about your other rituals, not a ritual itself — it benefits from unhurried, both-fresh attention, which only w7 reliably offers.

activities.name: Dreams Within Conflict
activities.one_liner: Gottman's approach to a stuck, recurring disagreement: instead of arguing the position, one partner becomes a 'Dream Detective' and asks questions to surface the deeper dream, value, or history underneath the other's stance.
how_it_works: Pick ONE specific, currently gridlocked issue — not a fresh argument, an old recurring one.
Decide who is the Dreamer (whose underlying dream/value you're exploring) and who is the Dream Catcher (asking questions).

The Dream Catcher asks open questions about the story and meaning behind the Dreamer's position — where it comes from, what it symbolizes, why it matters this much — without arguing or trying to change their mind.
The Dreamer tells the story as fully as they can; the goal is the Dream Catcher understanding, not agreeing.
This is explicitly NOT a problem-solving conversation — no compromise is attempted in this session.
Swap roles on a separate occasion for the other partner's side of the same issue.
activities.timezone_friction: Requires sustained emotional attention from the listener and enough safety/time not to rush a still-vulnerable story — this needs w6/w7-level commitment. See window_contraindications: actively wrong for w1 or w4, and w6 needs extra caution here specifically.

activities.name: Four Horsemen Self-Check + Repair Attempt
activities.one_liner: A quick before/during-conflict check against Gottman's four predictors of relational breakdown (criticism, defensiveness, contempt, stonewalling), paired with actively naming a repair attempt out loud.
how_it_works: Before a hard conversation, each of you checks: am I about to criticize (attack character) instead of complain (name a specific behavior)?
During the conversation, if either of you notices contempt (eye-rolling, mockery, sarcasm) — flagged as the most corrosive of the four — name it and pause.
If you feel yourself getting defensive, try owning a small piece of the complaint instead of countering.
If either of you starts to shut down (stonewalling), call a real break rather than pushing through flooded.
Explicitly offer or ask for a repair attempt at any point: a literal 'can we start over,' a touch, a joke, or 'I need this to be gentler' all count.
Give the repair attempt a real chance to land — Gottman's research finds repair attempts fail most often because the other partner doesn't recognize or accept them, not because they weren't offered.
tools_needed: Nothing beyond the call itself; optionally keep the Four Horsemen names written somewhere visible
activities.timezone_friction: A lightweight, always-available awareness practice rather than a scheduled sit-down, so it can be invoked briefly even in w4 (catch it before a lunch-break disagreement escalates) or w5. Not claiming w1/w6 — see window_contraindications; a real repair conversation needs more regulation than either partner reliably has in those windows.

activities.name: Hold Me Tight — The Seven Conversations (EFT)
activities.one_liner: Sue Johnson's book-based, DIY version of Emotionally Focused Therapy: seven sequential conversations that map your negative cycle, find the vulnerability under it, and rebuild attachment security.
how_it_works: Get the book 'Hold Me Tight: Seven Conversations for a Lifetime of Love' (Sue Johnson) — the conversations are designed to be worked through together with the book, not improvised from a summary.
Conversation 1, Recognizing the Demon Dialogues: together identify the repeating negative pattern you fall into (e.g., pursue-withdraw) without labeling either person as 'the problem.'
Conversation 2, Finding the Raw Spots: each of you names the old wound or fear that gets triggered in that pattern.
Conversation 3, Revisiting a Rocky Moment: pick one specific recent fight and walk back through it slowly, naming the softer, underlying emotions each of you skipped past in the moment.
Later conversations build toward directly asking for what you need and repairing specific past injuries, ending with naming rituals that keep the bond alive going forward.
One conversation in the sequence centers specifically on physical touch/bonding — that one does not translate to video and should be set aside for in-person time (see gaps).
tools_needed: The book 'Hold Me Tight' by Sue Johnson (paperback/ebook/audiobook)
activities.timezone_friction: Each conversation surfaces attachment fears and old wounds — needs both partners regulated and unhurried, which only exists in w6 (if deliberately chosen as worth the cost) or w7. Actively wrong for w1 and w4 — see window_contraindications.
activities.source_date: book originally published 2008; publisher page accessed 2026-08-02

activities.name: Imago Dialogue — Full Mirror / Validate / Empathize
activities.one_liner: A structured three-step turn-taking dialogue (Mirror, Validate, Empathize) for working through something that actually matters, not just a fun exercise.
how_it_works: Decide who sends first (has something to say) and who receives (listens).
Sender shares one thought/feeling in short chunks, not a monologue.
Receiver mirrors it back near-verbatim: 'If I got it, I think you said...' then asks 'Is there more?' until the sender says they're done.
Receiver validates: 'You make sense to me because...' — acknowledging the sender's logic, not necessarily agreeing with it.
Receiver names the feeling underneath: 'I can imagine you might be feeling...' and checks 'Is that how you feel?'
Switch roles — the new sender responds to what was just said rather than introducing a new topic — and repeat.
tools_needed: FaceTime video — seeing each other's face matters for this one
activities.timezone_friction: The receiver role is genuinely effortful — accurate mirroring plus validating plus naming feelings without editorializing takes real concentration — so this needs both partners alert. w6/w7 only, for the same reasons as the other full-conflict protocols; see window_contraindications.

activities.name: Imago Micro-Dialogue — Appreciation Only
activities.one_liner: The same Mirror/Validate/Empathize structure, restricted to something positive — a compliment, a thank-you, a good moment — so it's short and safe for public or hands-busy settings.
how_it_works: Sender shares one specific positive thing: an appreciation, a good moment from the day, a compliment.
Receiver mirrors it back in their own quick paraphrase: 'So you're saying...'
Receiver validates briefly: 'That makes sense' or 'I can see why that landed for you.'
Receiver names the feeling: 'Sounds like that made you feel proud/relieved/happy' and checks.
Optionally swap sender/receiver once more; stop whenever the window runs out — there's no vulnerable content left exposed if you're cut off.
tools_needed: Phone call or FaceTime audio — no screen required since there's no conflict content to read faces for
activities.timezone_friction: By restricting content to appreciation instead of conflict, this version is safe to interrupt mid-conversation — nothing vulnerable is left exposed if she has to cross a street (w3) or her lunch ends (w2/w4). This is the honest workaround for Imago: the mirror/validate/empathize STRUCTURE survives shortening, but the CONTENT must be downgraded from real conflict to something low-stakes to make it safe for a hard-stop window — the full-conflict version has no legitimate short form (see gaps).

activities.name: ECR-R Attachment Style — Solo, Then Compare
activities.one_liner: A free, validated 36-item questionnaire measuring attachment-related anxiety and avoidance; each of you takes it alone, then you compare and discuss results together.
how_it_works: Each partner takes the Experiences in Close Relationships-Revised (ECR-R) questionnaire independently and privately, ideally on your own free day.
Rate each of the 36 items on the 7-point agreement scale as it applies to close relationships generally (or this relationship specifically, if you prefer).
Note your two scores: attachment-related anxiety and attachment-related avoidance.

On your next call, share results and talk through what resonates — where your styles complement or clash, and whether either of you recognizes the described patterns in how you handle distance and reunions specifically.
Treat this as a conversation-starter, not a diagnosis — it's a research instrument, not a couples-counseling tool by itself.
activities.timezone_friction: Solo, self-paced, and resumable — a natural fit for the asymmetric free-day windows where one partner has unstructured alone time and the other is working; the comparison conversation happens later on a shared call.
activities.source_date: Fraley, Waller & Brennan, 2000 (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 78, 350-365); lab page accessed 2026-08-02

activities.name: Five Love Languages Quiz — With an Honesty Caveat
activities.one_liner: The popular quiz identifying a preferred 'love language,' included as a common shared reference point — with an explicit note that a 2024 relationship-science review finds weak empirical support for its core claims.
how_it_works: Each of you takes the free online Five Love Languages quiz independently, on your own time.

Compare results on a call and talk through whether the described language actually matches how you each prefer to receive care — treat it as a conversation prompt, not a verified fact about yourselves.
Use it to generate concrete requests ('I'd love more of x') rather than as a label to lean on.
Read the caveat together at least once — it changes how much weight to put on the result.
tools_needed: 5lovelanguages.com official quiz or equivalent free version
activities.timezone_friction: Same asynchronous-halves fit as the ECR-R entry — solo quiz on a free day, discuss together later.
activities.source_date: Impett, Park & Muise, 2024, Current Directions in Psychological Science

window_contraindications.reason: The escalating-disclosure design depends on finishing what you start — stopping mid-Set-III leaves the more vulnerable partner exposed with no landing. W1 risks starting Set III right as she's falling asleep; W4 guarantees a hard stop mid-protocol.

These conversations surface attachment fears and old wounds. Doing that with a sleepy, about-to-sleep partner (w1) or under a hard 60-minute cap with a return-to-work deadline (w4) risks flooding without time to re-regulate. W6 is usable only if deliberately chosen as the reason he's staying up — not as a default slot, since sleep deprivation impairs the emotional regulation this work requires.
Same logic as above: real content needs both partners regulated and unrushed. Use t5-imago-appreciation-micro instead in these windows.

Gridlock work asks the listener to stay curious and non-defensive about an old sore spot — a hard ask when exhausted. Unlike Hold Me Tight above, w6 is flagged here with no exception: a sleep-deprived nervous system is a worse foundation for this specific exercise than for a simple conversation. If he's staying up for w6, spend it on something lower-conflict.

window_contraindications.protocol: t5-gottman-state-of-the-union (State of the Union — concerns portion)
window_contraindications.reason: Parts 3-4 ask for real concerns and a request for change — that needs both people resourced. W1 and w4 don't give it time or alertness; w5 is asymmetric enough (one fading, one energized) that the 'both feel equally heard' premise of the meeting breaks down. Reserve for w7.
Requires holding visual attention on-screen for several minutes, which reads as conspicuously intimate and simply isn't possible mobile (w3) or plausible at a desk/in public (w4).

This one otherwise tolerates asymmetry well, but avoid w6 specifically: asking him to stay up specifically to listen to her vent about her day is a bad trade against w6's cost — save w6 for something that couldn't happen at any other time.

ldr_maintenance_research.finding: Long-distance dating couples show MORE idealization (idealistic distortion, romantic love, relational reminiscence, perceived agreement) than geographically close couples, and this idealization is associated with less frequent face-to-face contact. LDR couples are more stable than geographically close couples WHILE separated, but longer gaps between visits plus extreme idealization during separation predict instability upon reunion/cohabitation.
ldr_maintenance_research.source: Stafford, L., & Merolla, A. J. (2007). Idealization, reunions, and stability in long-distance dating relationships. Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 24(1), 37-54.
ldr_maintenance_research.relevance: Frames why this library should lean toward frequent, ordinary, low-idealization contact (parallel presence, mundane check-ins) rather than only curated 'special' moments — the research suggests over-idealizing the relationship during separation is a real risk, not just a cute trope.

ldr_maintenance_research.finding: Long-distance partners reportedly show higher intimacy and more self-disclosure than geographically close partners, attributed to 'behavioral adaptation' — LDR couples compensate for reduced face time with more intentional, deeper communication.
ldr_maintenance_research.source: Jiang, L. C., & Hancock, J. T. (2013). Absence makes the communication grow fonder: Geographic separation, interpersonal media, and intimacy in dating relationships. Journal of Communication (DOI: 10.1111/jcom.12029).
ldr_maintenance_research.relevance: Supports building the library around intentional, structured conversation (which this thread supplies) rather than assuming distance is purely a deficit to compensate for.

ldr_maintenance_research.finding: In a controlled comparison, romantic couples showed stronger prefrontal interpersonal neural synchrony and better behavioral coordination face-to-face than over video; the video-mediated advantage couples normally have over non-romantic pairs (friends) disappeared in video calls specifically, suggesting video restructures how couples connect relative to in-person.
ldr_maintenance_research.source: Published in Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience, 2025.
ldr_maintenance_research.relevance: Direct evidence for why protocols in this thread need real adaptation for video rather than an assumption that 'a video call is basically the same as being there' — most concretely, it strengthens the case for the eye-gaze closer (a low-cost way to recover some of what video strips out) and for keeping full-vulnerability protocols in windows where nothing has to be rushed.

thin_window_note: Directly served: w2 and w4 via t5-36-questions-set1-warmup, t5-gottman-love-map-single-question, t5-gottman-stress-reducing-conversation, t5-imago-appreciation-micro, and t5-four-horsemen-repair-checklist. w3 specifically via two audio-only, hands-free, no-screen entries (t5-gottman-love-map-single-question, t5-imago-appreciation-micro) that satisfy the W3/W4 hands-busy constraint explicitly. w8/w9 via the two solo-then-compare assessment instruments (t5-ecr-r-attachment-assessment, t5-love-languages-quiz-honest), per this brief's own must_cover direction that assessments suit the asymmetric free-day windows. NOT served, deliberately: I found no legitimate way to shorten a full conflict-repair or attachment-wound protocol (Dreams Within Conflict, Hold Me Tight, full Imago) into a genuine w2/w3/w4 form — the content itself, not just the duration, is the obstacle, and forcing a 10-minute version would misrepresent the protocol and could leave someone emotionally exposed against a hard stop. That is a real finding, not a shortfall: these protocols correctly stay w6/w7-only, and the appreciation-only Imago micro-version is the honest workaround (downgrade content, not just duration) rather than a fake shortened version of the real thing.
gaps: Gottman Relationship Checkup (337-item paid clinical assessment) was researched per the must_cover list but is DISQUALIFIED for this couple's use case: gottman.com states it 'is designed to be used with a therapist in a professional setting' and requires a clinician-sent invitation; partners cannot self-administer or compare results without a therapist. Not included as an activity for that reason. Source (opened directly): https://www.gottman.com/couples/checkup/.

No peer-reviewed study was found testing remote/video-call administration of the Aron et al. 36 Questions protocol specifically. The closest available evidence is a 2025 hyperscanning/fNIRS study on video-mediated vs. face-to-face communication in romantic couples generally (see ldr_maintenance_research), which is suggestive context, not a direct replication. UNKNOWN whether video changes the closeness effect of the 36 Questions specifically.

The provenance of the 4-minute eye-gaze closer commonly attached to the 36 Questions is contested: it is NOT confirmed to be part of Aron et al.'s own published 1997 methodology. Secondary journalism (Arizona State Press, 2015) attributes its popularization to Mandy Len Catron's viral NYT Modern Love essay, itself apparently drawing on separate mutual-gaze research (Kellerman, Lewis & Laird, 1989, 'Looking and loving,' Journal of Research in Personality — that original study used 2 minutes of gaze, not 4). I could not open either the original Aron 1997 full text (academia.edu returned HTTP 403) or the Kellerman et al. 1989 paper (ScienceDirect returned HTTP 403) to verify this directly. Confidence on this specific provenance claim: medium, sourced only to secondary journalism.

ICEEFT's own site (iceeft.com) blocked WebFetch with HTTP 403 on every page attempted (root, /hold-me-tight-for-therapists/, /hold-me-tight-materials/, /about-ceft/) despite being findable via search. The EFT/Hold Me Tight entry is therefore sourced to Sue Johnson's publisher (Hachette, opened directly) and a non-official secondary site (holdmetightseattle.com, opened directly) for the complete seven-conversation list, not to ICEEFT directly — this is why that entry is medium rather than high confidence. Worth a retry with a different fetch method if higher institute-level confidence is needed.

t5-imago-appreciation-micro (the 'appreciation-only' Imago adaptation) is my own reasonable extrapolation from the documented Mirror/Validate/Empathize structure, not a named, independently published exercise I found in the literature. The underlying three-step structure is well-sourced across multiple corroborating pages; the specific 'restrict content to positive material to make it thin-window-safe' framing is not independently published. Flagged distinctly from the high-confidence base structure.

The SAGE journal page for Impett, Park & Muise (2024) on love languages did not render full article text on direct WebFetch (returned only site navigation, not a 403 but not usable content either); the specific findings cited (love-languages typology weakly supported, '10 of 10 studies' failing to confirm Chapman's claims) are corroborated via the search engine's indexed snippet of that article plus one independent secondary source (psychiatrist.com, 'Study Refutes Concept of Love Languages') rather than a directly-read primary abstract. Confidence: medium, not high, despite the source being a genuine 2024 peer-reviewed review.

Media multiplexity theory (Haythornthwaite) was searched per the brief but could not be traced to a clean primary citation (year/journal) within budget — only a Wikipedia summary was accessible, and it makes no LDR-specific claims. Dropped from ldr_maintenance_research rather than presented as a sourced fact.

This thread's own brief lists thin_windows_you_own as w4 (micro) plus w6/w7 (long-form), but the must_cover section separately instructs that assessment instruments 'suit W8/W9, where each does their half alone on their free day.' I followed the must_cover instruction and tagged the two assessment entries w8/w9 rather than treating that as exclusively T2/T3/T6 territory — flagging this explicitly in case Research-Lead intended a stricter boundary; T5 owns the underlying assessment content regardless of which window it's used in.

Jiang & Hancock (2013): Wiley returned HTTP 402 Payment Required on direct fetch, so the primary abstract was not read directly — see ldr_maintenance_research entry, confidence marked medium there for that reason.
confidence_summary: MEDIUM-HIGH. Core protocol citations are solid: Aron et al. 1997 (SAGE journal page opened directly, HIGH for the study's existence/citation), seven of nine Gottman Institute sub-topics (gottman.com pages opened directly, HIGH), Fraley/Waller/Brennan 2000 ECR-R (opened directly from the primary author's own lab page, HIGH), and Stafford & Merolla 2007 on LDR idealization (SAGE page opened directly with full abstract, HIGH). Two structural issues pull the entry-level average toward medium: (1) ICEEFT's own site blocked every direct fetch attempt this session, so EFT/Hold Me Tight is sourced to the publisher and a non-official secondary site instead of the institute itself; (2) several psychology-publisher pages (both SAGE URLs used for love languages, and the original 36-questions/Kellerman papers) rendered navigation only or returned 403/402 rather than full text, so a few claims rest on search-engine-indexed snippets and secondary corroboration rather than a directly-read primary source. Every individual activity's confidence field reflects this per-entry rather than a uniform rating; the window_contraindications and the love-languages honesty framing are the two places this thread was specifically asked to prioritize honesty over completeness, and both are flagged accordingly rather than smoothed over.
